description: We are six SVNU students, building a web app that harmonizes NASA FIRMS MODIS and VIIRS hotspots into a clear burning-activity calendar for emergency responders, scientists, and land managers.
summary: BurnCal turns 25 years of NASA satellite fire detections into one comparable burning calendar. MODIS (since 2000) and VIIRS (since 2012) see fires very differently. VIIRS's finer pixels detect 2.4 to 8 times more fires, so raw counts jump when the sensors change and long-term trends become misleading. We count each fire once per ~1 km equal-area grid cell per day. We then convert MODIS into VIIRS-equivalent units with a factor fitted on 2012–2017, when both sensors were flying and before the MODIS orbits drifted. Days when a satellite failed are detected automatically and filled by the next-best sensor, or shown as "no data" instead of fake zeros. Tested on years it never saw, the method predicts within 2.7% for Brazil, 4.9% for Australia and 16.5% for Egypt, and every MODIS-era value carries a 95% uncertainty band. Users select any area on a map and get a monthly calendar from 2000 to 2025, each month compared with its historical median, plus a CSV of the underlying detections. Agriculture and environment agencies and researchers can see whether burning in a place like Egypt's Nile Delta is really rising or falling, instead of mistaking a sensor change for a trend.
details:
What it does. BurnCal answers a simple question: is burning in this area unusual compared with its own history? Pick an area on the map and choose a date range. You get a monthly calendar of fire activity from 2000 to 2025 on one consistent scale. Each month is compared with the median of the same month in other years and shown with an uncertainty band. You can also download the raw detections as a CSV.

How it works.

  1. Load. We read NASA FIRMS active-fire records from MODIS (Terra and Aqua), VIIRS S-NPP and VIIRS NOAA-20: 79 million detections, covering over 200 countries for 2025 and the full history for Egypt, Brazil and Australia. We keep only vegetation fires (gas flares and industrial heat are about 70% of Egypt's VIIRS hotspots) and drop low-confidence detections.
  2. Count the same way. Each fire counts once per ~1 km equal-area grid cell per day. This removes VIIRS's advantage of having several small pixels on the same fire.
  3. Convert. S-NPP VIIRS is the reference. MODIS is converted with a factor fitted on 2012–2017, when both satellites overlapped and before the MODIS orbits drifted. Egypt's yearly factor varies between 7 and 11 from 2012 to 2017, peaks at 14 in 2018, then falls to 4.4 by 2025. Fitting on recent years would cut Egypt's history in half.
  4. Uncertainty. Each factor has a bootstrap 95% confidence interval. Small areas lean on their country's factor, so a few fires can't give a wild result.
  5. Satellite outages. The pipeline finds days when a satellite failed, such as Terra's 18-day shutdown in June 2001, and uses the next-best sensor. Where no other sensor exists, the month is shown as "no data".
  6. Serve. A FastAPI service answers calendar, map and CSV requests in about 0.15 seconds for any area.

Benefits and impact. Agencies tracking crop-residue burning, haze and wildfire risk can trust long-term trends instead of being fooled by a sensor change. Researchers get a documented, reproducible method with its uncertainty stated. Every number links back to the raw NASA detections.

Tools. Python, DuckDB, FastAPI, Pydantic, SlowAPI and pytest (70 automated tests); React, TypeScript, Vite, Tailwind CSS and MapLibre GL JS with OpenFreeMap tiles; Git and GitHub. The full pipeline runs in about 2 minutes on a laptop with under 2 GB of RAM.

What's creative. We put both sensors on a common unit (fire cell-days on an equal-area grid). We chose the calibration window to avoid orbit drift. The changing yearly factor itself works as a diagnostic: drift matters for Egypt's small farm fires but barely affects Brazil's or Australia's large fires. And we show "no data" honestly instead of zero.

Factors we considered. Gas flares and other non-fire heat sources; differences in pixel size; satellite orbit drift; satellite outages; noisy factors for small areas; areas that cross borders where countries have records of different lengths; and running on ordinary laptops.
